title: Garbage collection: how would you investigate allocation and GC pressure?
description: Learn how to spot excessive allocations, interpret GC event counters, and use profiling tools to reduce GC pressure in .NET applications.

data.text: The .NET garbage collector reclaims memory that is no longer reachable, which frees you from manual memory management. But GC work is not free. High allocation rates cause frequent collections, CPU spikes, and unpredictable latency — especially in latency-sensitive services.
Investigating GC pressure means looking at three signals: allocation rate, GC pause duration, and heap size. If any of them are trending upward, you should trace where the allocations originate.

data.title: Signs of GC pressure
items: CPU usage spikes with no obvious business logic cause.
P99 latency increases while average latency stays flat.
Process working set grows steadily and never shrinks.
GC event counters show Gen 0/1 collections in rapid succession.

data.title: High allocation in a tight loop
data.content: This method allocates a new string for every item, even though the format never changes.

data.text: Start with lightweight event counters for direction, then move to a full profiler when you need stack traces. The goal is to identify hot allocation paths without stopping production.

data.title: Investigation steps
items: Watch `gc-heap-size`, `gc-fragmentation`, and allocation rate over a representative workload.
If Gen 2 collections spike, run `dotnet-dump` or Visual Studio Diagnostic Tools against a production dump.
Use PerfView or JetBrains dotMemory to collect allocation stacks and filter by type.

data.title: Production-safe profiling
data.text: Event counters and `dotnet-trace` are low-overhead enough for production. Heap snapshots and full debuggers are not. Use sampling tools first, and collect dumps only when you have a hypothesis.
After locating the hot path, reduce allocations by reusing objects, pooling buffers, and choosing value types where lifetime and size permit.

data.title: Reducing allocations
data.content: Reuse a single StringBuilder and return a pooled array when the caller only needs read-only access.

items.question: Should I always try to eliminate allocations?
items.answer: No. Premature optimization adds complexity. Profile first, then fix hot paths.

items.question: Is Span<T> the answer to all GC pressure?
items.answer: Span<T> reduces array copying and string allocations, but it is not a universal solution. Profile before rewriting.

items.question: What is LOH and why does it matter?
items.answer: The Large Object Heap stores arrays larger than 85,000 bytes. LOH objects are collected only during Gen 2, so frequent large allocations cause expensive pauses.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Use event counters and low-overhead tracers before taking heap snapshots.
Focus on allocation rate and Gen 2 collection frequency.
Reduce allocations on hot paths with pooling and reuse, not everywhere.
LOH fragmentation is a specialized but important cause of GC pressure.
data.takeaway: Measure allocation stacks, fix the highest-impact path, and verify with counters.
